title: Arjuna and the Wooden Bird
text:
Drona, the teacher of arms to the young princes of the Kuru family, wanted to test which of his pupils was truly ready. He had an artificial bird made and set it high in the top of a tree. Then he called the princes together and told them that each, in turn, would aim at the bird's head.

He began with Yudhishthira, the eldest. When the prince had taken aim, Drona asked him what he saw. Yudhishthira said he saw the tree, the bird, his teacher and his brothers. Drona asked him again, and he gave the same answer. Drona told him to step aside without shooting. He put the same question to the other princes one after another, and each described the tree, the bird, the people around him. Each was sent away.

Then it was Arjuna's turn. He drew his bow and Drona asked what he saw. Arjuna said he saw only the bird; not the tree, not his teacher. Drona asked him to describe the bird. Arjuna replied that he saw only its head, not its body.

Drona, delighted, told him to shoot. Arjuna released the arrow and cut off the bird's head, and it fell to the ground.
lesson: Before you act on a goal, narrow your attention until only the target remains. Everything else in view is a distraction you have chosen to keep.
people: Drona, Arjuna, Yudhishthira and the other pupils
caveat: In the Sanskrit text Arjuna sees only the bird's head; popular retellings say he saw only its eye.
